doc.title: Howie Shear interviewed by Monk Rowe, Dunkirk, New York, October 11, 2014

chapter: Jazz as a career and wrap-up
title: Jazz as an international language
summary: Learning jazz made friends in Paris and South America with Woody Herman and fed his teaching income and creativity.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Oh absolutely. Yeah, yeah, yeah. I think the greatest thing I ever did was learn how to play jazz. Two Augusts ago I was in Paris for two weeks. And when they hear you play, wherever it might be — this particular place was Paris — you just make friends immediately because it’s a language. And you might not speak French — but I happen to speak French so I got along great speaking French — but if I didn’t it wouldn’t matter because I speak jazz and all these jazz people who come out speak jazz, or they want to speak jazz and they love jazz. So you make friends right away, which means you always have a place to stay and you always have a place to eat, and people say — and this was the case when I was on Woody Herman’s band, we were in South America and I didn’t speak a word of Spanish in any dialect, and yet — and there was not a lot of English going on there. But these group of trumpet players, 10, 12, 15 of them, took me out to dinner every night and treated me so well. And I felt like I was at home. So it’s a language that I learned how to speak and it’s basically an international language. Everybody knows it, speaks it, wants to learn it, and it’s probably the single greatest thing I’ve ever learned. Plus most of my students are — they want to learn how to play jazz. I have some classical students and some students in orchestration, private students, but most, by-and-large most of my students, private students, want to learn how to play jazz, whether they are in eighth grade, or I have students in their sixties now and fifties who always wanted to do that, who are now kind of retiring so they could lose their job and then want to play jazz and it’s all about that. And if I didn’t learn how to play jazz that would have been a big part of my income that I wouldn’t have been able to do. So it’s the best thing I ever did was learn it. And I tapped into my own creativity. I think everybody’s creative and I think everybody needs to explore where they’re creative. If they just spend a little time seeking it out and asking themselves the right questions. Because as a classical player growing up, I didn’t think I was very creative. I thought okay I was a good trumpet player and I could play that and I could play that, and I might teach music. And then I said well let me see if I could do this thing. And then as I learned more and more and I spoke the language of jazz better and better, I said well I guess I have some creativity there.
